title: Ready for me (Berakhot 58a)
hookLine: Ben Zoma: Adam labored for bread; I wake and find it ready
carry: all this was done for me
tomorrow: what do you say to a friend you haven't seen in a year?

cards: Toast takes about one push of a lever. The bread was just there, in a bag, on the counter. So who baked your bread before you were even awake?

Ben Zoma, a sage of the Mishnah, stood looking at a great crowd and answered that question out loud. Blessed is the One who created all these to serve me. It sounds, at first, like a strangely self-centered thing to say.

teach.b: Then he explains. Look how hard the first man worked before he ate bread: he plowed, sowed, reaped, bound sheaves, threshed, winnowed, sorted, ground, sifted, kneaded, baked, and only then ate.
And I wake up and find it all ready for me. The same for clothes: shearing, washing, combing, spinning, weaving. All of it at my door in the morning.
So it isn't bragging. It's counting. Each step behind your bread is a person, and Ben Zoma names them one by one.

teach.h: THE GOOD GUEST, THE BAD GUEST.
teach.b: A good guest says: look how much trouble my host went to, and all of it for me. A bad guest says: what trouble? I had one piece of bread, one cup; he did it all for his own family anyway.
Here's a neighbor who looks at the same plate.
In the Qur'an, Muslims read: "Let man consider his food." And the passage goes on to the rain poured down, the earth split open, the grain made to grow.
That's shared: stop, look at what you're eating, and see the work behind it.

teach.h: ALL THIS WAS DONE FOR ME.
teach.b: And one honest difference. Ben Zoma counts the people, the plowers and the bakers, and thanks God for them. The Qur'an passage counts God's own work, the rain, the earth, the grain.

how: Jews bless God before and after eating, and in the grace after meals a guest adds a blessing for the host, much like Ben Zoma's good guest.

o: a sage boasting that the whole world was made just for him
waking to bread many hands made, and thanking God for them
a meal set out for the poor before anyone else is served

games.q: the bread and the guest — tap the pairs.
p: wakes and finds it all ready
look how much he did, for me

s: 'all this was done for me' is Ben Zoma bragging that he's special
he's counting the work of every person behind his bread, and thanking God.
Ben Zoma contrasts a good guest with a bad guest
the good guest sees the host's trouble; the bad guest says the host did it for himself.
the Qur'an's 'let man consider his food' and Ben Zoma say exactly the same thing
both look at the work behind food; Ben Zoma counts the people, the Qur'an passage counts the rain, earth and grain.

games.q: your aunt hosts the whole family for a holiday. on the drive home your cousin says, "she loves cooking; she'd do it anyway." which guest is your cousin being?
o: a fair guest: if the host enjoys it, there's no trouble to thank.
the bad guest: Ben Zoma's bad guest says the host did it for himself.
a good guest: he noticed she loves it, which is a kind of thanks.
games.why: Ben Zoma's bad guest says, what trouble did the host take? he did it for his own household. the good guest says, all this trouble, for me.

practice: Take the last thing you ate and count backward, on your fingers. Who sold it, who drove it, who packed it, who picked or milled it, who grew it. When you run out of fingers, keep going in your head.

wordCard.voice: Ready for me: Ben Zoma waking up to bread that a long line of people made, and blessing God for every one of them.

orig.note: Hebrew: prepared before me; Ben Zoma wakes to find it all ready.

carryVoice: Said like a good guest: all this was done for me. Thirty-eight of fifty, with thanks.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 58a (Ben Zoma at the Temple Mount: 'who created all these to serve me'; the labors for bread and a garment; the good guest and the bad guest)
Qur'an 80:25–27 (water poured down, the earth split, grain made to grow)
